title: Starting a company one rung at a time
headline: Conviction comes
one rung at a time.
lesson: You do not need every answer to begin. You need a clear next step.
excerpt: You don't need to start a company with total conviction. You just need enough to take that first step.

blocks.text: You don't need to start a company with total conviction. You just need enough to take that first step.

Conviction is often talked about as binary: you have faith in something or you don't. But when we started Gamma, it felt more like a series of rungs on a ladder. Instead of trying to jump to the top, we just had to figure out what step would let us reasonably believe we should keep going.
The first rung was figuring out if the three of us could work well together. It took us 5 months of trying things out to answer that question.
Then came the ability to tell an investor what we were trying to do, and a basic working prototype. Would anyone believe there was a chance we could make this work?
Then the first 4 hires. Could we get people to leave well-paying jobs in the tech industry, take a fraction of their old compensation, all on the chance their equity might one day be valuable?
Then public launch. Would strangers that didn't know us sign up for what we were building and keep using it?
We never thought, for example, that if we could get funded, we'd made it. Or for any other milestone after that. Each one just gave us the right to tackle the next challenge.
I think this is how you make a long start bearable. You don't have to believe in the whole journey from the beginning. You just have to know which rung you're on.

title: AI slide decks and communicating ideas
headline: The pitch
is the proof.
lesson: Time saved on formatting can be spent making an idea easier to understand.

blocks.text: I run the company responsible for a lot of the AI-generated slide decks out there now, and I agree with Sarah.

When we were building Gamma, formatting was the friction I was most interested in removing. In a previous life, I spent a lot of late nights making research look presentable, and most of that time was spent moving and aligning boxes. I wished I had more time to simplify my ideas so that they were easier for others to absorb.

Our first pitch deck for Gamma was a rough prototype of the product itself, a hybrid of doc and slides, interactive and media-rich. Many investors passed. But the ones who said yes trusted our belief about slides because the deck itself embodied it: the pitch was the proof.

Sarah elaborated on her fund's LP deck in a follow-up post. It featured "default formatting on white slides," she wrote, and she threw it together overnight. It worked because it "distilled years of human thought and experience into an opinion."

That opinion is the thing no model can do for you. The best AI deck starts with the thing only you can have: the customer call that changed your mind, the number you'd defend in a partner meeting, the bet that smart people think is wrong.
Whatever time AI saves on formatting your ideas, you should spend on simplifying how they get communicated.

Making content is easier than ever with AI, but earning attention and trust is still hard. Effective communication has become the bottleneck to innovation, and it's the problem Gamma exists to solve.

title: Superhuman and defining the target customer
headline: Know exactly
who you are for.
lesson: A precise audience makes it easier to decide what to build—and what to leave out.
excerpt: Rahul Vohra raised Superhuman's product-market fit score from 22% to 33% without shipping a single feature; all he changed was who he counted as his target market.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Rahul Vohra, founder of Superhuman, against a brick wall
images.caption: Rahul Vohra, founder of Superhuman, against a brick wall.

blocks.text: Rahul Vohra raised Superhuman's product-market fit score from 22% to 33% without shipping a single feature; all he changed was who he counted as his target market.

The score came from a startup survey: ask users how they would feel if they could no longer use it, and score the share who answer "very disappointed." Scored across everyone, Vohra's came back at 22%. He used those users' own words about themselves and the value they got from Superhuman to define the target customer.
Then he ran the math again counting only people who fit that description, and the score was 33%.

The new customer description created an almost uncomfortable level of detail. Their target was now someone who lives in their inbox, reads 100 to 200 emails on a normal day, typically sends 15 to 40 emails back, but as many as 80 on a busy day.
Counting fewer people might sound like gaming the numbers, but it came with a real decision: Vohra picked that one type of customer to build for, and said “no” to feature requests from everyone else.

You can copy Vohra's move without running a survey. Write down exactly who your product is for, in one sentence, and let that sentence decide which feature requests you turn down and which you pursue.
P.S. AI has made shipping features easier than ever, but that's only revealed the real cost of trying to please everyone: losing focus.

title: Mary Barra and remembering a crisis
headline: Some lessons
must stay with us.
lesson: A company’s values show up in what it chooses to remember.
excerpt: "I never want to put this behind us."
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Mary Barra in a General Motors executive portrait
images.caption: Mary Barra in a General Motors executive portrait.

blocks.text: "I never want to put this behind us."

Mary Barra said that to General Motors employees at a town hall in June 2014, five months into the job, with the company recalling 2.6 million cars over an ignition switch tied to dozens of deaths. She finished her sentence: "I want to put this painful experience permanently in our collective memories."
A retired GM executive later told Fortune it was unlike anything any previous GM CEO had said.

The normal way to handle a crisis is to close it: settle the claims, announce the reforms, and let everyone move on. Her own employees would have preferred that, and she stood in front of them and demanded the opposite.

She created a VP of Global Vehicle Safety role that had not existed before and put Jeff Boyer, a 40-year GM engineer, in it. She hired Anton Valukas, the former US Attorney who had examined the Lehman Brothers collapse, and told Congress he had free rein to go where the facts take him. She put Kenneth Feinberg in charge of a compensation fund that paid out roughly $595 million in claims.
Any competent board can hire an investigator and pay the victims.
Only a company with deep values decides to keep remembering what happened. No budget forces that choice.

title: Julia Hartz and learning to trust instinct
headline: Instinct is earned
in the quiet years.
lesson: Years of questioning can become the judgment that a difficult moment demands.
excerpt: "In order to get out of that room, that dark room, I had to go on instinct completely."
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Julia Hartz, co-founder of Eventbrite
images.caption: Julia Hartz, co-founder of Eventbrite.

images.alt: Portrait of Julia Hartz
images.caption: Portrait of Julia Hartz.

blocks.text: "In order to get out of that room, that dark room, I had to go on instinct completely."

That's Julia Hartz in the spring of 2020, when COVID took Eventbrite's quarterly revenue from $80.8 million to $8.4 million, and she had to make almost every decision with no precedent to guide her. There was no handbook for a pandemic.

She had been CEO for four years by then, and spent three of them doubting herself. Her husband and co-founder Kevin had run the company for its first 10 years, and she kept wondering whether she was qualified for the job or just doing it the way he would have.

In hindsight, those three years of doubting herself can look like wasted time. They also gave her instinct. You cannot make 100 fast decisions in a crisis unless you have already spent years working out, slowly and with some doubt, what your company is and what your job in it actually is.

She did her second-guessing in the calm, when the company was growing and went public, so by the time the crisis hit, none of it was left to slow her down. Most founders never get to work through it that early.

Her instinct pushed the company through its crisis. Revenue fell to $106.0 million for 2020 and climbed back to $326.1 million by 2023, and in March 2026 she sold the company to Bending Spoons for roughly $500 million.
I wonder how many people quit somewhere in year two of that feeling, just before the years of questioning start paying off.

title: The iMac and the work behind simplicity
headline: Simplicity takes
a little obsession.
lesson: The work behind an effortless experience is rarely effortless.
excerpt: To build the first iMac, Apple's design team went to a jelly bean factory.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Translucent blue Apple iMac G3 in the German plastics museum collection

images.alt: Bondi blue iMac G3 with matching keyboard and mouse
images.caption: Bondi blue iMac G3 with matching keyboard and mouse.

blocks.text: To build the first iMac, Apple's design team went to a jelly bean factory.

They were trying to make see-through plastic look appealing in an industry where every computer case was beige. The only people who had genuinely solved see-through color made candy. So the team studied how it was done, then worked with manufacturers in Korea to put it into a computer housing that cost 3x what a normal one did.
Jony Ive said simple products demand this kind of depth: "To be truly simple, you have to go really deep. You have to deeply understand the essence."

That is why the iMac came out with an almost effortless-looking design. Apple got to “effortless” by paying for work nobody would ever see: they studied a candy factory, coordinated with manufacturers in Korea, and paid for a case that cost 3x what a normal one did purely for the aesthetic.

Plenty of companies copied the see-through plastic afterward. Most skipped the factory visits and the extra cost that made it happen, and their versions looked cheap. The teams who got it right did the unglamorous, boring, on-the-ground work first.

title: Hiring when candidates use AI
headline: Ask them
to teach you.
lesson: A polished presentation is only useful when someone understands what sits behind it.
excerpt: We stopped trying to catch candidates using AI in interviews a long time ago. Now, we ask them to teach us something.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

blocks.text: We stopped trying to catch candidates using AI in interviews a long time ago. Now, we ask them to teach us something.

Everyone who interviews with us builds a presentation and walks us through it. They can use whatever they like to put it together (including AI and Gamma itself), and most people do. Using AI is just assumed now, like with a laptop.
What we are watching happens in the minutes after the slides go up, when someone has to explain the thing they just made to a room that keeps asking why.

You can tell almost immediately. Someone who understands their subject can teach it cold, take a question sideways, and keep going. Someone who has only assembled it can't, and no amount of polish closes that gap.
That is the whole test. It’s survived the tools getting increasingly scarily good because teaching is the one thing retrieval cannot do on your behalf.
It also clarified what we are hiring for. Judgment rather than recall. People who can take something ambiguous and own it, which turns out to be a generalist trait more often than a specialist one.
What would your interview loop look like if you assumed the language model was already in the room?

title: William Wrigley and discovering the real product
headline: The real product
was the free gift.
lesson: Watch what people actually value, even when it challenges the business you have built.
excerpt: In 1891, a soap salesman in Chicago found out his customers didn't want his soap. They wanted the free gift he'd been attaching to it.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: 1929 charcoal and chalk portrait of William Wrigley Jr. by Samuel Johnson Woolf
images.caption: 1929 charcoal and chalk portrait of William Wrigley Jr. by Samuel Johnson Woolf.
images.credit: Samuel Johnson Woolf / National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution; CC0

blocks.text: In 1891, a soap salesman in Chicago found out his customers didn't want his soap. They wanted the free gift he'd been attaching to it.

William Wrigley Jr. had been attaching free gifts to that soap for years. He once bought 65,000 cheap red umbrellas to give away with it. The red dye came off them in the rain, but they sold soap anyway, so he kept going: cookbooks, fishing tackle, lamps, razors, cash registers. Whatever he could attach to a sale, he tried attaching it.
Then he added baking powder. He was selling to shopkeepers, one order at a time, and before long they were ordering the soap to get the baking powder.
So he shut down the soap business. By 1892, he was selling baking powder, with two free packs of chewing gum thrown in on top.
You can guess how this goes. The shopkeepers did the same thing with the gum, so he shut the baking powder down too and built a chewing gum company instead.

I like to think about how the first one must have felt. You spend years learning to sell something, you get good at it, you build a business on it, and then you look at what's actually selling and it's the free thing in the box.

The easy version of this is a story about listening to customers, and I don't think that's what happened. Nobody wrote to Wrigley asking him for a gum company. His revenue kept insisting the answer was soap. What people take for free measures demand better than what they'll pay for, because it strips out everything a customer tolerates to get the one thing they actually came for.
Most founders I know are good at noticing this stuff. The rarer thing is acting on it while the old business is still paying everybody's salary.
What are your customers already taking for free that you haven't admitted is the product?

title: Marvel and financing its own films
headline: Bet on the story
you already own.
lesson: A constraint can become the starting point for a different business model.
excerpt: In 2005 a company fresh out of bankruptcy borrowed $525 million against its own superheroes.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark in the red and gold Iron Man armor
images.caption: Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark in the red and gold Iron Man armor.
images.credit: Marvel Studios / Paramount Pictures; via Los Angeles Times

blocks.text: In 2005 a company fresh out of bankruptcy borrowed $525 million against its own superheroes.

Marvel had filed for Chapter 11 in 1996, and it came out of it in 1998 into a strange position: it owned the most valuable characters in popular culture and made none of the films. Spider-Man belonged to Sony, X-Men to Fox, Hulk to Universal. Marvel collected a licensing fee while the studios kept the profits, and it spent the next seven years watching other people build franchises out of its own catalog.

David Maisel joined in 2003 to run a studio that made nothing, and his argument was that Marvel should stop renting out its characters and start financing its own films. The objection to that was obvious. These were films budgeted at up to $165 million each, and Marvel's entire company, comics and toys included, sold $390 million in 2005.

So he built the loan around the objection rather than arguing his way past it. Merrill Lynch put up $525 million to fund up to ten films, secured on the film rights to the ten characters nobody had licensed: Captain America, Nick Fury, Black Panther, Ant-Man, Hawkeye, Doctor Strange, Cloak & Dagger, Power Pack, Shang-Chi and The Avengers. Marvel put in no cash of its own, and if the films flopped the lenders took those ten characters and could touch nothing else in the company.

The first film off the slate was Iron Man, which wasn't even on the list. New Line Cinema had been sitting on those rights and let them go, so Marvel took them back and amended the facility in October 2006 to cover them.
Then came the casting. Robert Downey Jr. was a few years into a comeback the industry still treated as a risk, and the board wanted Timothy Olyphant instead, but Maisel pushed for Downey and got him.

Iron Man opened in May 2008, cost $140 million and made $585 million, and Disney bought the company sixteen months later for $4 billion. The ten characters a lender had once been ready to repossess became the core of a franchise that has since taken more than $30 billion at the box office.

title: Lisa Su and the AMD turnaround
headline: Find your strength.
Stay with it.
lesson: A turnaround can start by deciding what the company is already good at.
excerpt: By 2014, one of America's oldest chip companies had so little of the data center market left that executives rounded its share down to zero. Zero. The company was AMD.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Lisa Su, CEO of AMD
images.caption: Lisa Su, CEO of AMD.

blocks.text: By 2014, one of America's oldest chip companies had so little of the data center market left that executives rounded its share down to zero. Zero. The company was AMD.

AMD had already cut a quarter of its workforce, sold its Austin campus and leased it back, and spun out the chip factories it was built on. In 2012 it lost more than $1 billion in a single year, and an analyst publicly called it uninvestable. It would lose money every year from 2012 through 2016.

Revenue fell 28% in 2015, to $3.99 billion, on a net loss of $660 million. That July the stock touched $1.61 (yes, $1.61). The company carried about $2 billion in debt. At the end of 2014, all of AMD was worth $2.07 billion on the public market.

Lisa Su became CEO on October 8, 2014, and called it her dream job. She had three electrical engineering degrees from MIT and 13 years at IBM behind her, plus advice from a mentor there she never dropped: "You should run toward problems."

Her plan came down to three things: make great products, rebuild trust with customers, and simplify the business. Some board members wanted AMD to switch to low-power mobile processors, since PCs were shrinking and smartphones were taking off. Su said no. Her line to Time years later was very simple: "We needed to bet on what we were good at."

Nvidia, the company AMD is now chasing in AI, is run by her first cousin once removed. Su's maternal grandfather is the eldest brother of Jensen Huang's mother. They did not grow up together and did not meet until an industry event, well into their careers. Her line to Bloomberg: "No family dinner. It's an interesting coincidence."

Today AMD is worth more than $800 billion. Intel is worth about 
$470 billion. She inherited a broken balance sheet and one thing the company was good at. She decided in her first year what all of it was for, and then she stopped re-deciding.

title: Rolex and foundation ownership
headline: The freedom
to take your time.
lesson: The ability to think in years changes what a company can make.
excerpt: The biggest name in luxury watches has no shareholders, no way to buy it, and no one who can own it personally.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Hans Wilsdorf seated at a desk surrounded by early Rolex posters
images.caption: Hans Wilsdorf seated at a desk surrounded by early Rolex posters.

blocks.text: The biggest name in luxury watches has no shareholders, no way to buy it, and no one who can own it personally.
Rolex is not controlled by a family, a conglomerate, or a sovereign fund. It belongs to a private foundation in Geneva, and it has sat there for over 60 years.

In 1945, after his wife died and left him with no heirs, founder Hans Wilsdorf moved his company into a foundation. When he died in 1960, the company passed to that foundation entirely, where it has stayed ever since: unlisted and effectively impossible to buy.

Rolex makes about 1.24 million watches a year. It brings in more than 10 billion Swiss francs in sales. It holds roughly a third of the entire luxury watch market, and it has zero shareholders to answer to. Thousands of people show up to work in Switzerland every morning, and in the end they work for a deed signed by a widower who had no one else to leave anything to.

With nobody demanding the number move by Friday, Rolex can run an 11-story site, 6 floors of it underground, where it casts its own metal. It can polish every case by hand. It can take the years a patented rose gold requires, stabilized with platinum so the color holds, and release it when it is ready and not a quarter sooner. It can pour profits into a bridge across the Rhone and a cardiology wing at the local hospital, with no Rolex branding on any of it.

The waiting lists everyone talks about are real, and so is the reason for them. In one of the only on-record statements Rolex has ever made, the company said the scarcity is, quote, "not a strategy on our part." Every watch is assembled by hand, and the company refuses to lower its quality bar to build faster. It is even putting up a fifth factory, in Bulle, to make more watches, not fewer. The shortage comes from how the watches are made, and no shareholder can force a shortcut for a better quarter.
That is what a company no one can buy can do.

title: Ford and the loan that saved the company
headline: Borrow time.
Build a future.
lesson: Resilience depends on the room you build before you need it.
excerpt: "Bet the company" is a phrase that usually lives in a pitch deck. In late 2006, Ford put it in a loan document. To get the money, it mortgaged its own logo.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Alan Mulally, former CEO of Ford
images.caption: Alan Mulally, former CEO of Ford.

blocks.text: "Bet the company" is a phrase that usually lives in a pitch deck. In late 2006, Ford put it in a loan document. To get the money, it mortgaged its own logo.
The Blue Oval, Ford's mark since 1927, was the collateral. Default, and a group of banks would own the name.

Alan Mulally had been at Ford for a matter of months. He came from Boeing, where he spent close to four decades building airplanes. He had never built a car. And Ford was dying. It lost $12.7 billion that year, the worst in its 103-year history, $5.8 billion of it in the quarter he signed.

His plan was to rebuild the entire company. Close 16 plants and start designing cars people actually wanted. But Ford couldn't afford any of it. It expected to burn $10 billion just staying alive through 2009, plus another $7 billion on new product, before it earned a dollar back. And its debt was junk - nobody would lend it a cent unsecured.
So Mulally pledged the hard assets: the factories, tooling, and even the land under the buildings. Ford had never pledged its core operations before. Not once in the life of the company.
The banks wanted more. Citi, Goldman, and JPMorgan, the three leading the loan, demanded the Blue Oval too.
$23.5 billion is what Mulally was eventually able to borrow against all of it. He had his own name for the deal: the world's largest home improvement loan.
Bill Ford, the great-grandson of the founder, signed the papers that pledged the family name. He described the moment years later: "My heart stopped for a moment."
It would be five and a half years before Ford got the oval back.
At the time, the whole thing read as surrender. An outsider CEO pawning the crown jewels on the way down.
Then he did the part nobody asked for. He took more than the plan called for, and called the extra a cushion against a recession or some other unexpected event.

Two years later, the financial system fell apart. General Motors and Chrysler needed money and found there was none left to borrow. Every credit window on earth had closed, so they went to Washington because Washington was the only lender left. They took the bailout and went through bankruptcy.
Ford did neither. No bailout. No bankruptcy.
Mulally didn't borrow because he knew what was coming. He borrowed while he still could, and that made all the difference.
The "cushion" turned out to be the company.

title: Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal photograph
headline: Ordinary decisions.
An extraordinary story.
lesson: Work can matter in ways its makers could never have predicted.
excerpt: In 2007, a photographer was told to shoot one footballer and one kid for a charity calendar.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.alt: Lionel Messi holding baby Lamine Yamal during the 2007 charity calendar photography session
images.caption: Lionel Messi holding baby Lamine Yamal during the 2007 charity calendar photography session.
images.credit: Joan Monfort; via CNN / Yahoo Sports

blocks.text: In 2007, a photographer was told to shoot one footballer and one kid for a charity calendar.
The footballer was Lionel Messi. The kid turned out to be a 6-month-old baby named Lamine Yamal. On Sunday, in New Jersey, they play each other for the World Cup.

Robert Lewandowski (famous Polish player) saw the photo and almost refused to believe it was authentic. Photographer Joan Monfort told ESPN he had never believed in destiny before this and does now. But what makes the story stranger than destiny is how it actually happened.

Barcelona's foundation was producing a 2008 calendar with UNICEF. 12 months, 12 players, 12 children from Catalonia, all chosen by lottery. Yamal's parents, Sheila Ebana and Mounir Nasraoui, won a raffle in their neighborhood of Rocafonda, about 20 miles up the coast from Barcelona. Working class, heavily migrant. Fortune reported that studies suggest half the neighborhood lives below the poverty line.

No casting director picks that family. Messi got January because, as Monfort explained, he wasn't always in the starting 11. The most famous photograph in the history of the sport was handed to the squad player, paired with a baby found by lottery.
Take the story apart and the miracle disappears. What shows up instead is a sequence of ordinary decisions made by people who had no idea what they were building.

title: Lou Gerstner and the IBM turnaround
headline: Keep the pieces.
Change the culture.
lesson: Keeping an organisation together means making its people work toward the same customer.
excerpt: One of the greatest corporate turnarounds in history started with a new CEO refusing to do the one thing everyone told him to do.
provenance: User-supplied reading collection, 2026-10-23. Sponsored sections, newsletter navigation and emojis removed. Editorial headings and Qwarter takeaway added for this Stories collection.

images.caption: Executive portrait of Louis V. Gerstner Jr..

blocks.text: One of the greatest corporate turnarounds in history started with a new CEO refusing to do the one thing everyone told him to do.
In 1993, Lou Gerstner took over IBM. The company had just lost $8 billion in a single year. Investment bankers were pricing each division for sale. Nearly everyone agreed: break it apart.
Gerstner killed that plan. He believed the real value wasn't in IBM's individual pieces. It was in the ability to pull all of them into something a customer could actually use.

But keeping IBM together on an org chart was the easy version of that decision. Making the pieces actually behave like one company was the real work. And the texture of the dysfunction was almost hard to believe. Divisions ran as rival kingdoms. Units hid information from each other. Teams spent their days negotiating internal transfer prices instead of serving customers. The head of IBM's European business was quietly intercepting the new CEO's emails so his people wouldn't even read them.

And senior people had learned to preside over the work instead of doing it. Early on, Gerstner asked one of his top executives for a detailed breakdown of a money-losing business. Three days later, he asked how it was going. The executive said he'd check with his team and get back to him. Same answer the next time. And the time after that.
Finally, Gerstner cut him off: "Why don't you just give me the name of the person doing the work?"
The message behind moments like that was unmistakable. Stop presiding from a distance. Get into the actual problem. Point yourselves at the customer instead of at each other.

He followed through. He tied people's pay to how the whole company performed, not just their division. He built a services business selling customers the thing they wanted most: someone to make all the pieces work together. He changed who got promoted. "Culture," he wrote, "is the game."

blocks.text: Silicon Valley exists because one investor bet on eight scientists before they had a company, a product, or a plan.
In 1957, those eight men quit on William Shockley.

A Nobel laureate for helping invent the transistor, Shockley hired them to build the next generation of it south of San Francisco. He was brilliant, yet extremely challenging to work for. The stories were unreal, e.g., when a secretary cut her finger, he was convinced someone had done it on purpose and ordered the whole staff to take lie detector tests. When they asked Shockley's backers to replace him, the answer was no. So they left together.

Six of them held PhDs. They wanted one thing: a single employer willing to hire all eight as a group. No company would. Everyone wanted to buy technology, and nobody knew what to do with eight scientists who only came as a set.
Then a letter from the group reached Arthur Rock, a young associate at a New York investment bank.
Rock saw what the eight had missed about themselves. They were asking to be hired, but he decided to bet on them directly.
So he told them to stop looking for a job and start their own company, and then went to raise the money for it.
He pitched 35 companies. Each one said “no,” until, eventually, Sherman Fairchild said yes, and Fairchild Semiconductor was born with a $1.38 million loan.
Here's why the bet worked: People compound.

Fairchild itself became enormously successful. Then its engineers broke off to start their own firms, and those firms spun off more firms, until one company had seeded an entire region. The Valley still calls that family tree "the Fairchildren."

blocks.text: December 21, 2009. Domino's aired a national ad campaign that no sensible business would run. The campaign was titled: “The Pizza Turnaround.” It showcased real reviews and focus group reactions, all negative. It was the kind of stunt that could get someone kicked out of a marketing career.
But this ad had the opposite effect. They gave their critics a chance to speak, then spent 15 years proving them wrong.
Key figure: 23,500%
Domino’s stock surged from $2.29 in November 2008 to $540.43 in December 2021
The “Pizza Tastes Like Cardboard” Days

After becoming the biggest franchise-owned pizza chain in the late 1900s, Domino's made some aggressive financial moves in the mid-2000s. In April 2007, it borrowed $1.7 billion using future royalty and supply-chain revenue through a $1.85 billion debt facility. Then it used that money to pay shareholders a special dividend of $13.50 per share.

It was a clean piece of corporate finance for a chain whose revenue is almost entirely fees, royalties, and dough sold to its own franchisees. It also left Domino's carrying a heavily leveraged balance sheet just as the 2008 recession reduced takeout budgets. To make matters worse, it gave management little room to fund the one thing the brand actually needed: a pizza people wanted to eat.
By early 2009 the damage showed up everywhere at once. Domestic sales slid through 2008. The stock, which had priced its 2004 IPO at $14 a share, bottomed at $2.29 that November.

Focus groups told Domino's exactly why. Customers said the crust tasted like cardboard, and they weren't shy about saying it on camera. Other sessions dismissed the pizza as low-quality and forgettable. The chain spent a decade losing ground to Papa John's, Pizza Hut, and a wave of regional and fast-casual chains nobody at headquarters had taken seriously.
The problem started at the business structure. Domino's had roughly 8,700 stores in the U.S. and abroad. By early 2009 they ran almost entirely on independent franchisees.
Any recipe change affected a national supply chain built to manufacture and ship identical dough, sauce, and cheese to every store.

That kind of machine is built for consistency and speed at the cost of evolving tastes. For years it was simply easier to run another discount promotion than to touch the recipe, so Domino's, like its biggest rivals, competed almost entirely on price rather than on whether the pizza itself was any good.
Unfortunately, the pizza was not good.
To make matters worse, they faced a new market variable: the Internet.

In 2009, two employees filmed themselves contaminating food at a North Carolina store and posted it to YouTube. The video racked up more than a million views within days. It was Domino's first real lesson in how fast bad news now traveled. The old playbook of staying quiet and waiting for a story to fade became useless.
Rebuilding the Pizza in Public

Under CEO David Brandon, the turnaround began, with chief marketing officer Russell Weiner leading the charge. Weiner joined Domino's in 2008 from Pepsi's cola marketing team. Weiner's team spent 2009 pulling every damning line out of focus groups and social media, then built an entire campaign around it.

Pizza Turnaround, a four-minute documentary, was released on December 21, 2009. It features real employees seeing customers tear the product apart on camera. Weiner later described the strategy as an effort to blow up the bridge, so there was no path back to the old recipe or the old excuses.

After airing all the bad comments, they revealed the secret plan they had been working on for the past 2 years: a brand new pizza. A new sauce, a garlic-flavored crust, and real mozzarella instead of the processed cheese customers disliked.
The company rolled out the new recipe nationally the same week the campaign aired.

J. Patrick Doyle, then president of Domino's USA, became CEO on March 7, 2010, taking over from Brandon just as the first results came in. Doyle later admitted the campaign gave him a knot in his stomach on launch day, a fair reaction to airing your own worst reviews on national television.

The campaign leaned on transparency on all front. Domino's ran a live, uncensored Twitter feed on a digital billboard in Times Square, publishing praise and insults under the same hashtag. The internet that caused one of its crises is now its top promoter.
Then they implemented the Pizza Tracker. An industry first, it let customers track their orders in real time.

The results arrived fast. Domino's fourth-quarter 2009 net income jumped 114 percent, from $11.0 million to $23.6 million. Debt buybacks, an extra fiscal week, and stronger sales. Domestic same-store sales grew 14.3 percent in the following quarter, the biggest quarterly increase since the company's 2004 IPO.
Now that the Pizza was good, it was time to deliver it to as many people as possible.

Doyle's real bet was that ordering pizza should be as frictionless as the product itself. Domino's built AnyWare, a suite of ordering tools that let customers buy pizza by tweet, text, smart TV, smartwatch, or Ford's in-car system.

By 2015 digital channels were generating $4.7 billion in orders a year. That same year the company launched its first loyalty program, Piece of the Pie Rewards. To keep the system reliable, they made point-of-sale software and delivery logistics essential technology across all franchises. One JPMorgan analyst summed up the shift by calling Domino's a tech company disguised as a pizza company, a description close to how Doyle described it himself.
The Pizza That Ate The Hut

The results compounded for years. Domino's overtook Pizza Hut in 2017 to become the largest pizza company in the world by global retail sales. $12.2 billion versus $12.03 billion, a lead it has never given back.
By 2018, Domino's had strung together 30 straight quarters of same-store sales growth and tallied more than 60 percent of U.S. sales through digital orders.

The stock reflected it all: shares that bottomed at $2.29 in November 2008 closed as high as $540.43 in December 2021. That run outpaced Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Alphabet for several years. Financial media revisited this comparison so often it became a running joke about boring, reliable businesses beating glamorous ones.

None of it was a straight line, though. Inflation and a nationwide driver shortage hit hard in 2022: U.S. same-store sales fell 3.6 percent in the first quarter, the worst reading in over a decade, and net income dropped 22.8 percent as company-owned stores absorbed higher labor and food costs.
The stock, gave back nearly 38 percent that year. It reminded investors that even a well-run franchise system faces the same commodity and labor costs squeezing every restaurant chain.

The clearest sign of continued discipline came in 2023, when Domino's reversed a decade-long stance and partnered with Uber Eats. Management waited until aggregators were large enough that access mattered more than the pride of controlling every order.

Domino's negotiated exclusivity and kept its own drivers for the deliveries. By 2024 the partnership was still only 3 percent of sales, but executives pointed to it as a path toward roughly $1 billion in incremental revenue. After Uber Eats success, they added Doordash as a second aggregator in 2025.

By fiscal 2025, Domino's had made over $20.1 billion in worldwide sales from more than 22,100 stores across more than 90 markets. This was an increase from the $4.71 billion inwh revenue and $584.2 million in net income the year before.
Ninety-nine percent of those stores are independently franchised, the same structure that once made the original recipe so hard to fix.
Today, Domino’s holds a market advantage in the fast-food industry. All thanks to the willingness to admit things were wrong.
Key takeaways
Public confession only works once you've ‌fixed the product. Domino's used the apology campaign to introduce its new pizza. It took 2 years to get to that moment.

Franchise structure can be a liability and a moat. The same all-franchise system that made Domino's slow to fix its recipe in the 2000s became the engine that let it scale delivery fast, negotiate hard on Uber Eats terms, and keep 99 percent of stores locally owned while corporate focused on technology and supply chain.

Wait to compromise until the terms favor you. Domino's resisted third-party delivery apps for a decade even after competitors had signed on. They partnered with Uber Eats only once its scale let it negotiate exclusivity.

blocks.text: Roy Seiders built custom fishing boats for a living. He used coolers as casting platforms and makeshift seats. But the cheap big-box coolers were not built for anything other than holding a 6 pack. After getting tired of breaking his cheap coolers, he and his older brother Ryan decided to build one that could survive it.

What they built cost roughly ten times what Igloo or Coleman charged for a cooler the same size, in a category that had never had a premium tier. Seventeen years later, that single pricing decision is why YETI can post gross margins that look more like a software company's than a plastics manufacturer's.
By fiscal 2023, YETI was booking close to $1.7 billion a year in net sales at a gross margin near 57 percent. a business built almost entirely on the belief that a cooler is worth premium prices.
Key figure: 9%
YETI's net sales growth in the second quarter of 2026, with adjusted gross margin expanding to 59.5 percent
A Business Built to Be Cheap

Coolers were built to be replaced. Category leaders Igloo and Coleman had spent decades optimizing for the opposite of durability: injection-molded plastic, thin foam, hinges that snapped within a season. All engineered to hit a shelf price at Walmart or Target that a shopper wouldn't think twice about. Roy Seiders wanted something tougher than a typical Igloo or Rubbermaid, and he couldn't find one anywhere on the market.

That gap persisted for a structural reason. Big-box retail rewards the lowest landed cost, not the best-built product, and a manufacturer selling a $300 cooler through the same store as a $20 one would get buried on the shelf next to it. Nobody had a distribution model built to support a premium price, which is why the category stayed a commodity for decades even though every owner of a cheap cooler already knew exactly how it would fail them.

YETI proved that building a premium brand doesn’t exempt you from the price trap. Net sales fell 22 percent in 2017, wholesale volume alone dropped 40 percent, and the swing rattled investors badly enough that it became a headline risk in YETI's own IPO story a year later.
The Ten Times Rule

Roy and Ryan built the first Tundra cooler with a factory partner sourced through Ryan's fishing-rod business. They borrowed a rotomolding process from high-end Australian coolers, and priced the result at whatever it actually cost to build right. Roy later described the approach as a "10x rule": charge roughly ten times what a commodity competitor was asking. The higher price made the cooler more desirable. It’s the same effect that shows up in prestige goods. In 2012, private equity firm Cortec Group bought roughly two-thirds of the company for $67 million, funding the manufacturing and marketing that turned a cult product into a national brand.

The marketing strategy was also much different: instead of buying celebrity endorsements, YETI paid a growing roster of hunting guides, anglers, surfers, and pitmasters to use its gear and tell their own stories about it. The ambassador program started with two communities in 2006, fishing and hunting. By 2023 it grew to roughly 200 ambassadors across 15 communities., This “hidden” direct-to-consumer channel rose from 8 percent of revenue to 59 percent in under a decade. Selling straight to the customer meant nobody else could set the discount.

Holding a premium price also meant defending it in court. When RTIC launched in the mid-2010s selling near-identical coolers at half the price, YETI sued for patent, trade dress, and trademark infringement; the two sides settled in February 2017, with RTIC agreeing to pay YETI, stop selling the disputed products, and redesign its lineup. Three years later, YETI and Amazon jointly sued sellers of counterfeit Rambler mugs on the marketplace, and Amazon closed the sellers' accounts and refunded buyers. A ten-times price only survives if nobody can quietly sell an eight-times knockoff next to it.
The Luxury Stress Test

YETI went public on October 25, 2018, pricing shares at $18 and valuing the company at roughly $1.7 billion, below the range it had originally marketed to investors. The stock had a rough first two months, bottoming near $12 that December, before the underlying growth story took over: net sales climbed from $639 million in 2017 to $1.66 billion by 2023, at a 56.9 percent gross margin. By November 2021, the stock had run to an all-time high above $108.

The real test came in 2022. YETI recalled nearly 2 million Hopper soft coolers and gear cases after their magnet-lined closures could fail and release magnets that posed a serious ingestion hazard. The mess cost $128.9 million in operating income and dragged that year's gross margin down to 47.9 percent. YETI absorbed the hit, redesigned the product line, and rebuilt margin the following year rather than discounting its way back to volume.

The recovery held. Net sales reached $1.83 billion in fiscal 2024 and $1.87 billion in fiscal 2025, and by the second quarter of 2026 YETI was still growing sales 9 percent with adjusted gross margin expanding to 59.5 percent. The company has been funding its own growth ever since, backing a $450 million share buyback authorization with free cash flow instead of outside capital.

Drinkware, the category that made YETI a household name, now faces real competition from Stanley and Owala in an increasingly promotional market, and YETI's answer has been to keep expanding into bags, backpacks, and cookware rather than cut prices to defend share. The rule that started with a $300 cooler still governs a business worth billions: charge for what it's worth, and let somebody else fight over the discount bin.
Key takeaways

Use Price as a positioning decision, not a cost calculation. YETI's "10x rule" worked because a high price signaled durability and status. A cooler priced like a commodity would have been judged like one.

Owning distribution is the only way to protect a premium price. YETI's 2017 crash happened in the one channel it didn't fully control, wholesale. The fix was building a direct relationship with customers that nobody else could discount out from under it.

A moat needs upkeep, not just a moment of invention. Beating RTIC in court and absorbing a nine-figure recall weren't one-time wins. They were the recurring cost of staying premium, and YETI budgeted for both instead of treating them as emergencies.

$1.87 billion - YETI’s net sales in fiscal 2025

blocks.text: In December 2022, Carvana's bonds traded like the company had already filed for bankruptcy. A stock that hit $376.83 a year earlier had collapsed to $3.55, and the balance sheet carried $5.7 billion in unsecured debt against just $434 million in cash.

Eighteen months later, the same company posted an adjusted EBITDA margin no public car dealer in America had ever matched, built in part on the very acquisition Wall Street had blamed for nearly sinking it.
Key figure: 11.7%
Carvana's adjusted EBITDA margin in the third quarter of 2024, an all-time best for any public automotive retailer, paired with record quarterly net income of $148 million
The Acquisition That Nearly Killed the Company

For the whole pandemic, Carvana kept running the same playbook it had used for nine years. Sell more cars, grow revenue, and let margins wait. Then in May 2022, just weeks after used car prices topped out, the company closed a $2.2 billion all-cash acquisition of ADESA's U.S. physical auction business. To pay for it, Carvana issued $3.275 billion in new unsecured notes with a 10.25% coupon. The deal was supposed to be a play for scale. With prices already sliding, it became one of the riskiest moves the company could have made.

The timing could not have been worse. The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index fell 14.9% over the course of 2022, the sharpest one-year decline in the index's history, as the pandemic-era used car boom unwound all at once. Carvana had just leveraged itself to expand into a market that was shrinking underneath it.

The losses piled up fast. Carvana posted a $506 million net loss in the first quarter of 2022, then $806 million in the fourth, closing the year with a $1.6 billion loss and total liabilities near $9 billion. Cash on hand fell to $434 million. The company laid off 2,500 employees in May and another 1,500 in November. Roughly 4,000 jobs were cut in a single year.

By December, Carvana's corporate bonds were trading at roughly 40 cents on the dollar, yields had blown past 30%, and Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas said the stock could be worth as little as $1. Ten of Carvana's largest creditors, holding about 70% of its unsecured debt and including Apollo Global Management and PIMCO, signed a pact to negotiate as a bloc, the kind of move that typically precedes a bankruptcy filing. The stock fell to $3.55, and the market priced Carvana like it was already gone.
Turning the Biggest Creditor Into a Partner

When a group of creditors lines up against you, the usual move is to call the bankruptcy lawyers. Carvana went to work on its numbers instead. Through the first half of 2023, gross profit per unit set a company record every quarter. SG&A dropped by $1 billion on an annualized basis, and management got there a full quarter ahead of its own deadline. That gave Carvana something it hadn't had in a while: a real position to negotiate from.

The deal came in July 2023. Carvana and Apollo agreed to swap roughly $5.2 billion of unsecured bonds for new secured notes, and holders of more than 90% of the outstanding debt signed on. The exchange wiped out over 83% of the 2025 and 2027 maturities. Through payment-in-kind terms, it also cut annual cash interest by more than $430 million for two years. Bondholders got something for taking that hit. Coupons went up to as high as 11%, from the old 4.875% to 5.875%, and in return they received a senior secured claim on Carvana's assets, ADESA's real estate included.

That last detail mattered more than the headline interest rates. The ADESA network, the same $2.2 billion deal Wall Street blamed for nearly sinking Carvana, was 56 sites and 6.5 million square feet of reconditioning capacity that one Wedbush analyst had called an albatross. Once pledged as collateral, it stopped being the liability that caused the crisis and became the asset creditors wanted to protect. Instead of selling off the property that triggered the panic, Carvana used it to convince bondholders that keeping the company alive was worth more than forcing it into court.

Carvana never stopped cutting costs, but it drew a clear line around what it protected. Headcount and marketing shrank while the reconditioning network and inspection centers, the physical infrastructure behind every dollar of gross profit per unit, stayed fully intact. Every dollar saved went toward proving the unit economics worked before the company chased volume again, a sequencing choice that shaped everything that followed.
The Most Profitable Car Dealer in America

The debt exchange only bought Carvana time. What it did with that time is what built the business. Full-year 2023 gave the company its first annual net income, $150 million, along with record Adjusted EBITDA of $339 million. Part of that was flattering, since a one-time $878 million gain on debt extinguishment padded the bottom line. But every quarter showed real operating improvement underneath it, and in about a year Carvana went from burning cash to generating it.

2024 is when it stopped being debatable. Third-quarter net income hit $148 million, and that was the third profitable quarter in a row. The Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 11.7%, which Carvana says is the best any public automotive retailer has ever put up. Then came the full year. Revenue hit $13.67 billion, up 27%, net income reached a record $404 million, and Adjusted EBITDA came in at $1.378 billion.

The margin is what matters here. CarMax, the country's largest used-car retailer, posted an Adjusted EBITDA margin of roughly 4% in its fiscal year ended February 2025, and Sonic Automotive finished calendar 2024 at about the same level. Carvana ran at more than twice that. Two years earlier, the market had priced this business as if it were headed for liquidation. Now it was the most profitable public automotive retailer in U.S. history as measured by adjusted EBITDA margin.

And Carvana still owns only a small slice of the fragmented U.S. used-car market, so there's plenty of room left to grow. It kept building on the same foundation through 2025 and by December that year had rebuilt enough market value to join the S&P 500. Getting in takes four straight profitable quarters and a market cap above $22.7 billion. Three years earlier, Carvana had $434 million in the bank and couldn't have pictured clearing that bar.
Key takeaways

Turn your biggest creditor into your negotiating partner. When a small group of lenders holds enough debt to force a bankruptcy filing, fighting all of them at once is a losing strategy. Carvana let Apollo become the counterparty on a new secured-debt structure instead, trading higher interest for survival. Any company facing a concentrated creditor base should ask which lender benefits most from the company staying alive, and negotiate with that one first.

Protect the asset that caused the crisis, if it's actually the moat. Wall Street wanted Carvana to dump ADESA, the network behind its debt spiral. Carvana kept it, borrowed against it, and put the money into rebuilding reconditioning capacity. Some costs only buy you time. Others are the reason customers pick you in the first place. Carvana could tell the two apart, and that's why it recovered instead of shrinking.

Prove the unit economics before you chase growth again. Carvana sat on its growth plans until gross profit per unit and Adjusted EBITDA margin actually worked. Only then did it start scaling. Growth bought before the margins are there usually falls apart the first time the market turns. Carvana avoided that by doing things in the right order.

$2.2 billion - ADESA U.S. auction acquisition

blocks.text: In October 2015, Chipotle was the best growth story in American fast food. It had convinced the country that fresh, minimally processed ingredients could scale to two thousand restaurants without sacrificing speed. But then customers started getting sick. Five separate outbreaks within five months, followed by a multi-year collapse in sales, profit, and investor trust that took a new CEO and a rebuilt supply chain to fully reverse.
Key figure: 1,100%+
How much Chipotle's stock gained from its early 2018 low near $255 a share to its pre split all time high of $3,283 in June 2024
The Cost of Being Handmade at Scale

Chipotle's entire brand was built on a structural choice most large restaurant chains had abandoned decades earlier. Instead of a handful of processed, shelf stable ingredients moving through a handful of centralized commissaries, Chipotle sourced from hundreds of local and regional suppliers and had employees in nearly every restaurant hand cut vegetables, marinate meat, and prep produce on site. That decentralization was the entire "Food With Integrity" pitch. It also meant food safety protocols lived in thousands of individual kitchens instead of a handful of factories, with far less standardized kill steps for pathogens than a typical fast food supply chain relied on.

This lack of standardized safety protocols started showing consequences in the summer of 2015. 234 customers and employees got sick from a norovirus outbreak in Simi Valley, California. And during that same window, Minnesota health officials traced a salmonella outbreak tied to tainted tomatoes across 22 Chipotle locations. But it didn’t stop there. Merely two months later, Chipotle was forced to close 43 restaurants in Washington and Oregon, after an E. coli O26 outbreak spread across 11 states, sickening 55 people. Right after that (December 2015), an additional 130 Boston College students got sick from yet another norovirus outbreak. Public health officials estimated almost 500 people fell ill from Chipotle food in the second half of 2015 alone.

The market reaction moved just as fast. Chipotle's stock, which had hit an all time high of $758.61 a share on August 5, 2015, went into a slide. "Food With Integrity," the famous slogan that built Chipotle’s brand had become the headline of every negative story written about it. As a result, January 2016 marked the worst month in the company’s history since it went public, when comparable sales collapsed 36.4 percent.
First Rebuild the Kitchen, Then the Brand

Chipotle's first move wasn't an ad campaign. In December 2015, the company brought in food safety expert Mansour Samadpour and his consultancy, IEH Laboratories, to redesign its entire farm-to-fork process. The result was a program built around DNA based, high resolution testing of produce before it reached restaurants, new central kitchen prep for items like tomatoes and shredded cheese, and blanching for onions and other produce, along with new marination protocols for chicken and steak. Suppliers who couldn't meet the new testing thresholds were dropped. None of this made for good advertising. All of it was necessary before advertising could work again.

The company paired the fix with a very public accountability moment. On February 8, 2016, Chipotle closed all of its nearly 2,000 restaurants for four hours so co-CEOs Steve Ells and Monty Moran could walk every employee through the new protocols on a live broadcast. It bought the company little more than a news cycle. The first marketing move was an animated short called "A Love Story,", the second was a loyalty program called Chiptopia that gave away roughly $70 million in free food over one summer. Both moved people who were already die-hard fans, but failed to convince others Chipotle was safe again.

The fix that came last was the real needle-mover: Chipotle had been run by a co-CEO structure since 2009. But this structure isn’t effective at making fast, unified calls when a crisis occurs. In February 2018, the board switched the plan and hired Brian Niccol, the executive behind Taco Bell's own turnaround, as sole CEO. Shares jumped 11 percent on the announcement. Instead of re-litigating the food safety program that was already built, Niccol operationalized it and paired it with a mobile app overhaul, the Chipotlane drive through format for digital pickup.
The Slow Payoff

The recovery took longer than expected. Throughout 2016, comparable sales fell 20.4 percent, revenue dropped 13.3 percent to $3.9 billion, and net income collapsed 95 percent, from $475.5 million in 2015 to $22.9 million. Chipotle posted its first quarterly net loss in its history as a public company in the first quarter of 2016. Even in 2017, as one-year comps turned positive again, the two-year stacked comparisons that actually measured recovery stayed negative, and a single norovirus scare at one Virginia location that July was enough to knock the stock down 15 percent in a day. The stock finally bottomed near $255 a share in early 2018, down two thirds from its 2015 peak, right as Niccol's hiring was announced.

From there the business compounded. Chipotle's stock gained nearly 50 percent in Niccol's first full year, its best performance since 2013. Revenue climbed from $4.5 billion in 2017 to $11.3 billion in 2024, net income reached $1.53 billion, more than triple the pre-crisis peak. Digital sales barely existed during the crisis, but by 2024, they made up 35 percent of food and beverage revenue. By June 2024, the stock closed at a pre-split all-time high of $3,283 a share, prompting the company's first ever stock split.

The government took longer to close the book than the market did. In April 2020, Chipotle agreed to pay the Department of Justice a $25 million criminal fine, the largest ever in a U.S. food safety case. The risk of Chipotle not being perfectly safe didn’t fully disappear either. Just this summer, a salmonella outbreak was traced to a third party jalapeño supplier, sickening 345 people across 27 states. Chipotle’s stock reacted with a near 10 percent dip to the news. A new food safety program reduced the odds of another crisis happening, but it could not completely erase them.
Key takeaways

The model that built the brand also broke it. Chipotle's decentralized, hand prepped, minimally processed food was the entire "Food With Integrity" pitch, and it was also why five different pathogens could hit the chain in five months. Any business whose differentiation is "less standardized than everyone else" needs safety engineering that is equally non standard, not a bolt on fix.

Fix the supply chain before you fix the marketing. Chipotle spent over two years on unglamorous DNA testing and central kitchen changes before letting a campaign talk about trust again. Chiptopia and "A Love Story" moved loyalists in the short term, but the stock didn't move for good until two year comps turned durably positive under new leadership.

One accountable executive beats two in a crisis. The co-CEO structure that built Chipotle couldn't make the fast, unified calls a crisis demanded, and the stock kept falling for two years under it. Replacing it with a single outside CEO who had a proven turnaround record did more in twelve months than joint leadership had managed in two years.
By the numbers
~500 - People sickened in the second half of 2015
36.4% - Chipotle restaurant sales decline in January 2016
20.4% - Full-year 2016 comparable restaurant sales decline
$25 million - Criminal fine paid by Chipotle to the DOJ in 2020
1,068 - Chipotlanes open by the end of 2024
1,100%+ - Stock gain from the 2018 low to the June 2024 pre-split high

owning your oddness.

blocks.text: In 2008, Crocs’ stock tanked from the high $60s to about a dollar a share, and the brand became shorthand for a fad that had already died. But in 2021, the same ‘fad’ was posting a higher operating margin than Nike!
Key figure: 29.5%
Crocs' full-year 2021 GAAP operating margin, nearly double Nike's roughly 15.6 percent that same fiscal year
A Shoe Company That Kept Trying To Be Something That It Wasn’t

Crocs came into the market as a slip-resistant boat shoe all the way back in 2002. It was made from a proprietary closed-cell foam called Croslite. It caught on fast: by 2007 the company had introduced more than 300 different styles and a 2006 IPO to peak annual revenue of $847 million. Management read that success as proof Crocs could become a full lifestyle brand, and pushed into dress flats, wedges, golf cleats and boots, categories with nothing to do with what had actually made the clog work.

But when the recession hit, Crocs’ diversification didn’t make things easier for them. In 2008, Crocs lost $185 million and its stock collapsed from the high $60s to about a dollar a share. “They’re dead and they don’t know it”, said one hedge fund manager, describing Crocs as a walking zombie. The company managed to become profitable again by 2010, but despite that, leadership kept insisting on diversification. They kept adding SKUs throughout the early 2010s.

By 2013, Crocs kept widening its product range. However, this resulted in them having a catalog streched thing across categories where they had no real design edge. They fought a losing battle with Nike, Sketchers, and legacy fashion brands instead of simply defending their patented molded clog which nobody else could copy. Growth was masking the actual problem, which was that Crocs kept spending its scarce marketing and design dollars fighting battles it had no business fighting.

The major shift happened that December, when Blackstone invested $200 million for two board seats and a 13 percent stake in the company. In the following 12 months, Crocs had cut more than 180 jobs, closed around 100 of its 624 stores, and binned around 35 percent of their underperforming styles. The company refocused on their molded footwear line that had once generated $847 million on its own.
Cut Everything, Then Make People Beg for What's Left

Andrew Rees arrived at Crocs in 2014 as brand president, straight from L.E.K. Consulting, where he had helped write the turnaround plan he was now hired to run. He was named CEO outright in June 2017. His first moves weren't about brand voice. They were structural: close roughly 160 more stores, about 28 percent of the global fleet, between 2014 and 2018, and by August of that year, shut down Crocs' last owned factories in Mexico and Italy, moving to a fully outsourced model where the company ships Croslite pellets and steel molds to third-party manufacturers instead of owning plants.

That discipline showed up in the internal targets before it ever showed up in headlines. On the company's Q2 2018 earnings call, management set goals of a gross margin in the low 50s and SG&A in the low 40s as a percent of revenue, a cost structure most footwear brands never reach. And Crocs kept doubling down on what made them special. By the third quarter of 2020, clogs alone made up 72 percent of footwear revenue, up from 62 percent a year earlier. Betting on the core product compounded rather than plateaued.

Crocs’ second major move was the one people remember the most: turn the shoe's reputation for being ugly into the reason to want it. Starting in 2018, Crocs began dropping limited-run collaborations, tiny batches, real artists, prices near $60, and let scarcity do the marketing a big campaign budget couldn't. Post Malone's first clog sold out in 10 minutes and immediately resold for as much as $900 on eBay. Bad Bunny's glow-in-the-dark drop sold out in 16 minutes in September 2020, with pairs reselling for up to $300. Justin Bieber's drew house collaboration sold out that October, and a second Bieber drop the following March sold out in 90 minutes. None of these drops moved meaningful unit volume on their own. What they moved was perception: each one generated free press, reset the base clog as culturally alive instead of a punchline, and fed a resale market that made simply owning a pair feel like winning something.

The third leg was almost invisible and arguably the highest-leverage move of all. Crocs had bought a tiny accessory company called Jibbitz for $10 million back in 2006, and under Rees it became the way Crocs sold newness without touching its factory-free supply chain again. Instead of designing new shoe styles, the habit that had nearly killed the company twice, Crocs could release new charms instead. By 2022, Jibbitz accounted for 8 percent of company revenue and had grown 27 percent year over year, most of it dropping straight to the bottom line on a five-dollar plastic charm.
From Punchline to the Best Margin in Footwear

The strategy had already proved its worth, producing four straight years of growth by 2020. Then the pandemic hit, and everything was amplified. Working from home and comfort culture brought a wave of new fans to the brand. Crocs closed 2020 with record revenue of $1.386 billion, up nearly 13 percent, with operating margin climbing to 15.4 percent from 10.5 percent the year before. That was already the best year in company history. But it didn’t stop there.

In 2021, revenue made another massive jump, this time to $2.313 billion (up 67 percent in a single year), with gross margin expanding to 61.4 percent, and operating margin nearly doubling to 29.5 percent. This operating margin put it ahead of Nike, which ran roughly 15.6 percent that fiscal year. In 2020, Crocs sold about 69 million pairs of shoes; in 2021, it sold 103 million pairs, more than doubling net income to $725.7 million.

This time, Crocs was careful not to repeat its 2008-era mistake of chasing every category at once. In 2021, it paid $2.5 billion for HEYDUDE, a second casual footwear brand, funded mostly through cash and debt. The core Crocs brand kept compounding afterward, crossing $3.28 billion in 2024, up 8.8 percent, even as HEYDUDE itself fell 13.2 percent the same year on oversupply, a reminder that the original discipline (do one thing exceptionally, resist becoming everything) is easier to preach than to repeat inside a newly bought brand.

What survived is the playbook, not just the shoe. Crocs still runs on a $50 product, sold direct wherever possible, refreshed constantly through five-dollar charms and expensive-feeling celebrity drops instead of a bloated design calendar. The company once dismissed as a joke now runs one of the highest operating margins in an industry full of much bigger names, and it got there the same way it survived twice before: by doing less, better.
Key takeaways

Subtraction as a strategy, not a retreat. Crocs' comeback started with closing stores, cutting 30 to 40 percent of its SKUs, and shutting down its own factories entirely, before a single celebrity collaboration ever launched. Cutting first freed the capital and focus that made everything after possible.

Scarcity can replace a marketing budget. Post Malone, Bad Bunny, and Justin Bieber didn't move much volume directly. But they convinced the public that limited runs vanished in minutes and resold for hundreds of dollars, repositioning the brand better than any traditional ad campaign could have.

The highest-leverage move is often the smallest one. A $10 million accessory company bought in 2006 turned into an 8-percent-of-revenue, high-margin business that let Crocs sell newness constantly without ever redesigning the shoe or opening another factory.
By the numbers
$1.386 billion - Crocs' record revenue in 2020, up nearly 13% year over year
$2.313 billion - Crocs' revenue in 2021, up 67% in a single year
29.5% - Crocs' full-year 2021 GAAP operating margin
160 - Crocs retail locations closed between 2014 and 2018
72% - Share of Crocs' footwear revenue from clogs in Q3 2020
10 minutes - Time it took Post Malone's first Crocs collaboration to sell out in December 2018

to belong.

blocks.text: If you don’t know Skool, it’s a company founded by Sam Ovens (aka “The Henry Ford of consulting”) that allows users to create and monetize online communities.

What makes Skool so rich as a case study isn’t just that it’s the market leader in its space, but the unconventional (yet still highly methodical) manoeuvres that allowed the company to ascend as fast as it did.

After analyzing 1,000+ of Skool’s ads, combing through 18+ hours of video & interviews, and examining 85+ of their launch emails, I picked out the biggest and most important needle-movers that took Skool to 25 million users, a team of more than 240 people, and a platform valuation of $80 million after just 4 years of being open to the wider public (and without taking a single dollar from institutional venture capital).
The market opportunity presents itself:
Cutting revenue from $36M to less than $10M, and
downsizing the team from 45 to 6
Sam Ovens founded Skool with the grand goal of helping 1 billion users find and monetize their passion through online communities.

Before starting Skool, Sam was actually already running a very successful e-learning platform called Consulting.com, selling high-ticket courses to aspiring consultants, which he scaled to $36M a year… from scratch!
(He shelled out somewhere between $300k and $1M for the domain name alone!)
Yet, he decided to throw all of that away in order to pursue a completely new venture.
At a glance, that seems crazy.

In fact, when talking about this seemingly unreasonable early bet, Alex Hormozi, the wildly popular business guru who would later join the company as co-owner, says, “That’s where Sam just has these massive balls.”
To what extent that’s true, I’ll let you decide along the way.
But whether blind courage played a factor or not, there’s no denying that Sam had a very smart plan.

You see, Sam Ovens wasn’t just some off-the-grid hustler. In the late 2010s, he was regarded as the info product guru, and was dubbed “the Henry Ford of consulting” for making consulting, a profession normally available only to the elite, accessible to the masses.
The Henry Ford of consulting, at his office desk. Circa 2016
In just about 4 years, his Consulting.com company scaled from 0 to mid 8-figures, experiencing fantastic growth… but this massive growth came at a cost.

Due to the company scaling so fast, Sam hired 45 people in a very short span, and added a lot of things to the business, like posting on all social channels, many different funnels, many traffic sources, and a bunch of people making up a bunch of teams.

It was a total mess. Operations were chaotic, profit margins were thin, and there were always fires to put out in the company. Sam had to work harder and harder to keep Consulting.com afloat until he eventually got tired of running this kind of hectic business and took a much-needed break to figure out how to restructure his company.
“It felt like I was selling my soul to the content creation machine in order to feed my company and just to pay my expenses… What’s the point if I don’t enjoy it?”
During the sabbatical, Sam decided to tackle the problems his company had by using the Lean Thinking philosophy — an operating approach that focuses on maximizing value while minimizing waste.

In his case, Sam defined “value” as things that 1) help his clients, 2) get him money, and 3) bring him joy (aka, are fun to do). On the other hand, he defined “waste” as simply everything that couldn’t be categorized as value.

“I looked at every part of Consulting.com and tried to define whether it is value or waste. Value is something that improves the customer’s experience — it is defined by the customer. Only a few people in my company were customer-facing. 80% of my company was doing something related to paid advertising! Then I analyzed the flows of money. Most of it went into ads. But are ads valuable to the customer? No. And I was like, oh shit, that’s pretty bad.”
So how did he reorganize things for maximum effect?

To start, Consulting.com didn’t generate client results as well as it could have because it was working with too many people. So they stopped working with beginners and focused only on existing business owners to optimize for client results and happiness.

“We dropped our Consulting Accelerator product, and I decided to just focus on existing business owners. We now help coaches, consultants, course creators, and experts achieve $100,000 a month in profit with only one to two products, two to three remote staff, happy clients, and happy founders.”
However, this new modus operandi demanded drastic changes.
Sam shrunk the team from 45 to 6. He eliminated almost all of their traffic sources (Instagram, Facebook, etc.).
They even stopped running ads, on which they used to spend between $30k and $40k every day.

“So I basically got rid of 80% of the company, cut paid advertising to 0, and had a small team of 4-5 people that were all touching the customer, and we found a way to get the customer organically just by running really good programs, getting people really good results, and sharing that as our content strategy.”
After substantial cuts, the company now had only 2 offers, 1 funnel, and 2 traffic sources (YouTube and email newsletter).
The result? Despite revenue falling by more than 70%, Consulting.com was way more profitable. In one of the following months, they made $800,000, with $60,000 in expenses — the rest was pure profit.
So… happy days, right?
Not exactly.
A company like Consulting.com (that sells courses and helps people on the internet) needs three core components to function:
1. A content portal, or an LMS (learning management system),
2. A community where students interact, comment, help, and meet each other,
3. Scheduled live Q&A calls for coaching, so students can show up and ask questions.

In Sam’s case, he was using Kajabi for LMS, Facebook Groups for community, and Zoom for Q&A calls. But trying to get all of these things to work together was super annoying because they were completely separate, different things.

The students had to log in to Kajabi to watch the course. They had to log into Facebook to hang out with other students (while trying not to get distracted by cat videos and other interruptions that pop up all the time on Facebook). And trying to get people from all over the world in different time zones coordinated for Q&A calls was also a problem.
If you think about it, this fragmentation is considered a “waste” through the lens of Lean Thinking. Sam had to come up with a solution to reshape it into “value”.
It was an issue that needed to be addressed, but there weren’t any tools that took care of this.
As Sam put it: “I'm experiencing this problem, and it kind of sucks. I can see the solution in my head. Screw it, I'm just going to build a company and solve my own problem”.

And solve his own problem he did. He built a platform that served as an LMS, a community, and a calendar with live Q&A calls all in one. He named it Skool and became his own client with Consulting.com.

“It basically takes these three major pieces: your course & content portal, your community, and your event schedule, and it puts them into one simple tool that your students can access with one login and one unified search.”
But as soon as Sam started Skool, a different problem popped up: his attention was simply split too much between the two companies.
Sam had to make a sacrifice.

a blank page can be.
